title: Making nonlinear dynamics look linear: lifts, snapshot fits and low-dimensional models
summary: Koopman lifting, dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and latent Neural ODEs share one idea: find coordinates in which a linear or low-dimensional description is enough, and then check that it is.

media.alt: Line chart titled exact toy lift, add the observable x squared. Horizontal axis dimensionless time 0 to 3, vertical axis state from 0 to 1. An orange curve decays from 1 (x); a blue curve starts at 0.3, rises slightly to about 0.33 and then decays (y). Black open circles from the lifted linear model lie exactly on the blue curve.

read_the_figure.question: Does the reduced (linear or low-dimensional) model reproduce the full dynamics, and has closure been shown or assumed?
read_the_figure.axes: Lift chart: time against states x and y. DMD chart: x against y phase plane with a spiral and circles. POD charts: a space-time field (colour = value) and a bar chart of squared singular value share against mode number. Diagram slides: boxes from state to observables to linear evolution, and encode to latent ODE to decode.
look_at: Lift chart: solid curves are the nonlinear reference; black circles are the lifted linear model. They coincide: adding the observable x squared makes this toy exactly linear.
Slide 20 diagram: state (x, y), observables (x, y, x squared), then 'linear evolution?' with a question mark; the caption says finite closure must be demonstrated.
DMD chart: the black spiral is the reference snapshots; the orange circles are a rollout of a one-step linear map fitted to the snapshots; they sit on the spiral.
POD charts: the left field is a synthetic space-time pattern; the bar chart shows that two modes carry about 0.92 and 0.08 of the energy and the others almost nothing: two modes reconstruct this toy.
Slide 24 diagram: encode, latent ODE, decode; the caption says compression must preserve predictive information.
read_the_figure.proves: If circles lie on the curves, the reduced model reproduces the toy. These toys are chosen so that it is exact; the diagrams add the warning that for a real problem a finite lift or a handful of modes is a hypothesis to be tested, not a result.
if_wrong: Circles off the curve: the lift is not closed, or the snapshot spacing and the fit are inconsistent.
A slowly decaying bar chart: the field has many significant modes; a two-mode model would be wrong.
A latent state that cannot be decoded back to the original variables: information was lost in compression.
A DMD rollout that spirals out although the data spiral in: eigenvalues of the fitted map lie outside the unit circle.
must_check: That the reduced model is compared with the reference on data not used to fit it.
That the energy share of discarded modes is stated.
That the lift's closure is shown by an equation, not only by a plot.
That a latent model reports reconstruction error as well as prediction error.

terms.meaning: A function of the state, such as x squared; Koopman methods evolve observables instead of states.
A finite set of observables whose time derivatives are linear combinations of themselves.
Dynamic mode decomposition: fit a linear one-step map to snapshot pairs by least squares.
Proper orthogonal decomposition: the singular-vector basis that captures the most energy of snapshots.
An ODE for a compressed state z, with an encoder and a decoder at the ends.

remember: A lift is exact only when the observables are closed under differentiation.
DMD fits a linear map; it is exact only for linear dynamics or a closed lift.
Energy share of a POD mode is its squared singular value over the sum.
Compression is justified by reconstruction and prediction error, both.
A plot where the model matches the toy is a check of the code, not of the method on a real problem.

steps.title: The toy lift in equations
steps.note: Differentiating z = x squared gives -2 x squared: no new variable appears, so (x, y, z) obeys a closed linear system. This is consistent with the curves (x decays like e^-t, and y peaks near t = 0.2 at about 0.33).

steps.title: Solution for y
steps.note: Computed from the linear system; it reproduces the blue curve's initial rise to 0.33.

steps.title: DMD least squares
steps.tex: A=X'X^{+},\qquad x_{k+1}\approx Ax_k,\qquad \text{eigenvalues }\mu_j\ \text{of }A\ \text{give growth and rotation}
steps.note: X holds snapshots, X' the same shifted one step. A spiral inward corresponds to complex eigenvalues of modulus less than one.

steps.title: POD from the singular values
steps.note: The truncation error is the sum of discarded squared singular values, which is why the bar chart suffices to decide how many modes to keep.

worked.title: Is the lift closed?
worked.problem: For x' = -x, y' = -2y + x^2, differentiate z = x^2 and say whether (x, y, z) is closed.

solution.text: All three derivatives are linear in (x, y, z).

worked.answer: Yes: a three-dimensional linear system reproduces the nonlinear toy exactly.

analyze.q: Why does the lifted model reproduce y exactly in the toy, and what would go wrong if the equation had x cubed instead of x squared?
analyze.hint: Derivative of x cubed introduces a new variable.

analyze.q: The POD bar chart has two bars. How many modes do you keep for a 99 percent energy target, and why?

evaluate.q: A lifted model with six observables matches your data. Is that evidence of closure? What would you test?
evaluate.hint: Held-out initial states and longer horizons.

evaluate.q: What does slide 24's caption demand of an encoder?

create: Design a lift for x' = -x + x^3 type dynamics and say what happens to the closure.
Plot the singular values of the toy field on a log axis and propose a threshold with a stated error budget.

checks.q: What is the purpose of adding x squared?
checks.answer: To make the set of observables closed under differentiation, so the evolution is linear.

checks.q: POD shares 0.92 and 0.08. Truncation to one mode keeps what fraction of energy?
Why do DMD circles lie on the black spiral?
checks.answer: The toy snapshots come from a linear system, so a least-squares linear map reproduces them.

checks.q: Does a match on toys justify using DMD on a turbulent flow?
checks.answer: No: closure must be shown for that problem; nonlinear dynamics generally need many observables.

checks.q: Add a figure that shows when a latent model has lost information.
checks.answer: Plot decoded versus original variables for held-out data and the error against latent dimension.
